> The cards in AH, I found, mostly fix up what I had found to be problems in

> deck up to par with the bleed deck and the vote deck. While this could

...to which I would respond that Vote needs to hope that the whole table
isn't powerful enough to disagree (two vote decks at a table can really
hurt each other, while two combat decks only hurt each other when they
fight), and S&Bs versatility is almost nil.

> Secondly, the amount of effort
> needed to counteract a combat deck is much lesser than the effort needed
> to make a combat deck work, i.e. an ounce of combat avoidance is worth a
> pound of combat. Mind you, this is not something I wish to debate, this

> non-local Jyhad experience I have had), out of the 20 or so decks I saw
> myself and the other 20 or so decks that were seen by my cohort, we saw
> only 1 combat deck, and that was some "Zip Gun/Dragon Breath Round"
> monstrosity that I don't even consider a honest combat deck. I don't know
> if this was a result of a problem, or a symptom of a problem, but there it
> was.

The Zip Gun/Dragonbreath Rounds is (IMHO) one of the few card combos
which shouldn't exist. Real zip guns couldn't fire DB rounds (or
anything all that special, really).

> All the problems you pointed out about celerity, I basically agree with,
> but there have always been good ways to deal with celerity, be it sending
> them to torpor before they get to use their additional strikes or playing
> with Skin of Steel. The Nosferatu (or other Brujah) could always get away
> with Immortal Grapple and big hits, hoping that the Brujah was relying on
> Blur rather than stacked Potence strikes but the Gangrel could do nothing
> but try to not die as they Dodge and multi-strike.

Ahh, but for the Celeritous to have had that dodge, either they were
stacking dodge cards in their hands (and thus using up their deck
space), or were using Acrobatics for a single offensive strike. In
either case, they were emminently dealable in a Gangrel Deck that could
press to next round.

> The Tremere never have
> been as good at combat as they could have been, which is indeed made up
> for by their versatility, but it would be nice to be able to make a
> Tremere deck that could fight effectively.

I've never really seen a problem. Dodge, press. With a mob connections
or hawg, a lot of Tremere have vicious threat power. Gangrel can be
afraid to deal with them, as so much of their damage prevention is
ineffectual. Brujah can dodge that first strike each round, but for each
dodge they throw in, that is one less offensive strike they are doing...

> I guess, all in all, I agree with WOTCs development of the game. At some
> point they realized that Sneak and Bleed was too easy to get away with,
> and so they added stuff to fix that.

...they tried to fix that "problem" and horribly failed (IMHO). Of the
new anti-bleed cards in VTES, only Elder Intervention is a successful
card. Justicar Retribution and Archon Investigation are both too
powerful, and neither make sense as for "game-world reality". S&B was
eminently dealable with a huge amount of methods.

> I guess now they have realized what
> I have known all along, that combat was too difficult to make work
> (relative to voting or bleeding), so thay have added stuff to fix that.

> I am viewing the release of AH trough the eyes of a player in a group that
> has evolved the combat deck to an art form, and in doing so, have found
> all the big (and small) flaws with the various clans on that level. AH,
> we have found, patched these up and made us happy.

I've been happy with AH up to one point... I'm not sure if I like the
ramifications of Scorpion Sting. As a card just for Nossies, I might
have had no qualms, but I foresee some problems with Scorpion Sting, Dog
Pack, Wolf Claws. (I'll withhold judgment til I see it in play...)

> Jyhad is still a game where you can buy a couple of starters, a hand full
> of boosters and play with, but in that enviornment, you will end up with a
> bunch of people playing Malk S&B decks.

Actually, My experience in league play is that most people make mongrel
decks (here are a sample):

Malk/Tor/Ven Sneak&Bleed
Gan/Ven Bruise&Vote
Gangrel Bruise
Giovanni Bruise&Vote
Malk Sneak&Combat
Nossie Bruise&Bleed
Tor/Bru Bruise&Vote
Auspex Intercept&Runaway
Tremere Bruise

There was only one S&B deck (One Starter, Three Boosters, Three Vampires,
free trading environment)

> Then everyone will want to buy
> more cards to try to deal with that and work from there. If they go out
> and buy some AH, more power to them :-)

Hmm... Once S&B started cropping up in our regular playcirlce (soon after
starting), it was quickly dealt with by Deflection and Rush decks. Many
(me, for example) settled on light deflection for the big bleeds, and
never blocking (hand jam...). S&B is still occasionally around (and
usually the first recourse to newbies), but people soon find out that
while it is effective, it is not really any more effective than anything
else, and it is almost certainly less fun/satisfying.

From: Thomas R Wylie <aa...@cats.ucsc.edu>

> Dark Sovereigns was the first expansion for V:TES, and we played it a bit
> conservatively since it was unclear what the impact of an expansion would be.
> While it is true that the average card power is ramping up slightly, this is
> not aimed at catering to the munchkins. A weak card set is a boring card set;

A weak card set is not a boring card set. A weak card set is a poorly
tested card set. Being not weak, does not equate with being very strong,
however.

> I doubt that even a fourth of the Fourth Edition card set is used tournaments,
> for example, and one would think that more like a third of the basic set
> would appear in tournaments. Also, if we stop printing "wallpaper" cards,
> which everyone seems to be in favor of, then the power level will escalate
> by definition.

Not true. Removal of "wallpaper" will not escalate anything. The
removal of Concealed weapon and its replacement with a balanced card
escalates nothing. On the contrary, while it increases breadth, the
general power level of everything remains at the same level.

> It was recognized early on that a trading card game can't help but escalate
> slightly over time, as new cards make existing strategies slightly more
> efficient, unless the designers actively try to tone things down. What we
> don't want is for the power level to be making quantum jumps following the
> release of an expansion, which I don't think has happened with either
> Ancient Hearts or Alliances.

One has other options with expansions:
Introducing new styles of decks... This was done very
effectively with Assamites (a new way of fighting), and Setites
(corruption) and the DS clans were both finally given a true flavor in AH.
Making sure that each particular card has an appropriate cost.
Scorpion Sting, for example, negates the most common defenses against
combat, the dodge. In addition, hand strikes become more powerful. A
cost of 1 blood would make me have absolutely no qualms about a Dog
Pack/Scorpion Sting/Wolf Claw deck.

Messages.Body:
The Corrupter <sull...@cslab.uwlax.edu> wrote:
>> Dark Sovereigns was the first expansion for V:TES, and we played it a bit
>> conservatively since it was unclear what the impact of an expansion would be.
>> While it is true that the average card power is ramping up slightly, this is
>> not aimed at catering to the munchkins. A weak card set is a boring card set

>A weak card set is not a boring card set...

If the cards in a set are so bad that nobody really wants to put them in their
decks, but would rather stick with existing cards, then the card set is weak,
and boring. Even a high enough percentage of such cards makes the overall
card set weak on average.

>> Also, if we stop printing "wallpaper" cards,
>> which everyone seems to be in favor of, then the power level will escalate
>> by definition.
>
>Not true. Removal of "wallpaper" will not escalate anything. The
>removal of Concealed weapon and its replacement with a balanced card
>escalates nothing. On the contrary, while it increases breadth, the
>general power level of everything remains at the same level.

Of course it escalate the game. The old card was never used; the new card
is. Therefore, we have replaced one card with a better one, and the game
has escalated, though maybe not by very much. Replace several cards in the
same way, and the overall set definitely escalates. The same principle
applies to comparing the worst cards of one set with the worst cards of the
previous one.

>> It was recognized early on that a trading card game can't help but escalate
>> slightly over time, as new cards make existing strategies slightly more
>> efficient, unless the designers actively try to tone things down. What we
>> don't want is for the power level to be making quantum jumps following the
>> release of an expansion, which I don't think has happened with either
>> Ancient Hearts or Alliances.
>One has other options with expansions:
> Introducing new styles of decks... This was done very
>effectively with Assamites (a new way of fighting), and Setites
>(corruption) and the DS clans were both finally given a true flavor in AH.

But creating new styles of decks will inevitably lead to at least minor
escalation, since it's just not possible to allow playtesting to explore
*all* possible ramifications of a new deck style, if we want to release
expansions more than, oh, once a year.

> Making sure that each particular card has an appropriate cost.
>Scorpion Sting, for example, negates the most common defenses against
>combat, the dodge. In addition, hand strikes become more powerful. A
>cost of 1 blood would make me have absolutely no qualms about a Dog
>Pack/Scorpion Sting/Wolf Claw deck.

And again, there isn't time to make sure that every card is at exactly
the right cost, and several cards wind up seeming like they're worth
X-and-a-half cost anyway, with no obvious way to round the card effect up
or down without making it hopelessly narrow and/or complex.

In short: escalation will happen as long as expansions are put out. We can
make every effort to minimize the damage, but there's just no way to stop it
entirely unless we deliberately make bad expansions.

Howdy, Corrupter-san,

I'm not sure that the Scorpion Sting/Dog Pack Gangrel deck is really all
that scary as use of new cards goes, as it is something that could already
be done. A Gangrel who uses SS/DP is basically using 2 cards, one of
which is a fragile and expensive ally, to not quite have the effect of
Immortal Grapple (yeah, yeah, I know, I know. Shut up about the Immortal
Grapples already :-). Using IG prevents all strikes but hand strikes for
the entire combat and if the vamp presses, it is automatically at close
range. SS/DP does not prevent the opponents use of offensive strikes
(i.e. they can still Blur with a Magnum), the opponent can still attempt
to manuver to long range to avoid aggro Wolf Claw strikes. The opponent
can manuver to long range on the first round, shoot the Dog Pack with some
ranged damage, and then Dodge/S:CE on the second round or even as an
additional strike. If I manage to get you at close range and Immortally
Grapple you, you can do nothing but sit there and get hit for some
rediculous ammount of hand damage, which can very well be aggro (many
vamps have both Protean and Potence, and most of them are Gangrel. I can
think of 6 Gangrel with Potence off the top of my head). You can't dodge,
you can't S:CE, you can't use Guns, you can't use Thaumaturgy strikes, you
can't do anything but punch me (and I will win a punching fight). At
least with SS/DP, the defending vampire has some options and possibilities
to fight. With Immortal Grapple, they usually don't. Even against other
hand damage combat decks, the Celerity decks usually rely on multiple
small (Torn Signpost) hits rather than big stacked ones, which doesn't
help if you can't dodge the opponents first strike and you are sent to
torpor imediately, and the Gangrel usually only do 1 point of damage per
strike, which can be stopped by Flak Jackets.

Yes, SS/DP screws any deck that relies solely on Dodge/S:CE as combat
defense, but Immortal Grapple already did that, and SS/DP is much harder
to use than IG. SS/DP requires a good card combo in hand, the expenditure
of pool for the killable (or stealable or Cryptic Missionable) Dog Pack,
and the opponent not having more manuvers than you. SS/DP just makes it
so the Dodge/S:CE deck must put more thought in their combat defense.
Maybe they could go with Fortitude, or Flak Jackets, or Manuvers rather
than trying to Majesty out of everything. Again, as in most aspects of
Jyhad, it pays to be flexible and not too reliant on one deffense.

As for the Tremere, the Dodge/Press concept never quite works out as
nicely as it sounds. The Dodges are countered by Multiple Strikes, the
presses are put down, the opponent S:CE out of combat, or the Tremere is
Immortally Grappled :-)

On an entirely different angle, I am interested to hear why you are so
unfond of the new bleed-screw cards. I am not particularly bothered by
them, myself. Archon Investigation exisiting just means that you
shouldn't bleed some one for more than 3 unless you are sure that they
can't play AI (i.e. they have already played an OOT master, you have had
the chance to see their hand, whatever). 3 points a bleed is perfectly
sufficient to make a S&B deck work, and if you want to bleed for 7, you
should have to take the gamble. I can see Protected Recources being kind
of viscious if used by a Vote deck, but it won't help them at all if their
preadator is a non-bleed deck (just like AI). Yes, bleeding can be dealt
with by conventional means, but the Nosferatu, Brujah, Gangrel, Ravanos,
Setities, and Assamites can neither bounce or effectively intercept an
effective S&B deck (animalism intercept is not quite as good at stopping
massed stealth as Auspex is), and while all these clans can fight, putting
all your effort into fighting a S&B preadator means you are not hurting
your prey, and you are just making it easier for your grand-preadator to
gain 6 pool and then come for you next. At least with the threat of AI,
the S&B deck needs to not kill quite as quickly.

>in the sense of little strength, a weak card set is nothing more than a
>badly tested card set. "Boring" has nothing to do with weakness. They
>are mutually exclusive.

A weak card set is one that is underpowered. It may be the result of bad
testing, it may be the result of bad design.

>> Of course it escalate the game. The old card was never used; the new card
>> is. Therefore, we have replaced one card with a better one, and the game
>> has escalated, though maybe not by very much. Replace several cards in the

>inclusion would not be an escalation of power. Spawning Pool is costly,
>a unique, and only useful in certain circumstances.

Escalation can mean either increasing the average card power, or increasing
the maximum card power. Stopping escalation of the latter sort is
relatively easy, and generally desirable, but the occasional card will
still slip through the cracks. Stopping escalation of the average card
power is impossible without deliberately making bad cards that nobody
plays with, which is sort of missing out on the point of expansions.

>> But creating new styles of decks will inevitably lead to at least minor
>> escalation, since it's just not possible to allow playtesting to explore
>> *all* possible ramifications of a new deck style, if we want to release
>> expansions more than, oh, once a year.

>of the new clans id sn introduction, not an escalation. It is difficult
>to escalate something that never existed. In terms of whole game
>escalation, the introduction of quietus runs parralel to a
>Thaumaturgy/Protean combat deck, and its power level seems equivalent to
>a number of other combat decks. Again, no escalation, merely more
>breadth. Setites S&B is less powerful than its dominate based kin, but
>gives back more benefits (pool return).

Obviously you can't escalate something that didn't exist (unless you
consider creation to be escalation), but this threat is about the escalation
of the overall card set, or so I thought. New clans are definitely part of
the overall card set, and if the new clans are more powerful than the weakest
of the existing clans, then by introducing them, you have escalated the
general card set.

And judging power isn't always easy. For example, as you point out,
Setite stealth/bleed decks are different than existing ones. If it turns
out that gaining pool for bleeds more than compensates for the loss in
sheer bleeding power, then the new clan has just escalated the
stealth/bleed strategy.

escalation as I do (the increase in power on all levels of a general
strategy) then you are quite wrong. The escalation that I am worried
about can be avoided, or at the very least minimalized. AH did a
relatively good job at this, but I am worried by the tone you set in this
thread. It seems as though you are willing to "settle" on a set that has
minor escalation. Escalation can only lead to an inevitable collapse of
balance.

On 18 Jun 1996, PDB6 wrote:

> On an entirely different angle, I am interested to hear why you are so
> unfond of the new bleed-screw cards. I am not particularly bothered by
> them, myself.

Overall, their poor design. S&B may have been good, but not any better
than any other strategy in NL. While the basic concept (a stealth card and a
bleed card) made for an easy to get off combo, the S&B deck was never
robust, and setting it up to defend against rush/bleed bounce/intercept
watered down its strength. Not setting up for these defenses was a
surefire way to death. While there is one exception, the rest...

> Archon Investigation exisiting just means that you
> shouldn't bleed some one for more than 3 unless you are sure that they
> can't play AI (i.e. they have already played an OOT master, you have had
> the chance to see their hand, whatever). 3 points a bleed is perfectly
> sufficient to make a S&B deck work, and if you want to bleed for 7, you
> should have to take the gamble.

ARCHON INVESTIGATION
Archon Investigation has a huge problem: insufficient cost. For 3 pool,
the bleed against you fails, you use a master phase, and you burn a
predator's vampire. While this is one of many cards that could sit in
your hand (like Return to Innocence or Far Mastery), the cost is not
applicable. No matter what, you are losing less pool than if you took
the bleed (and burning a vamp - I had to say it again). More appropriate
would be:
Cost 1, the bleed is successful (i.e., still pool loss, they get Edge)
Cost x, bleed not successful (x is amount of bleed)

> I can see Protected Recources being kind
> of viscious if used by a Vote deck, but it won't help them at all if their
> preadator is a non-bleed deck (just like AI).

Protected Resources is TOO effective a card for the cost. At least it
could be a location. In a vote deck, this is not a wasted card. Unless
no one at the table has any bonus bleed cards/bleeders (highly unlikely)
it will be useful.

Justicar Retribution is awful too, though. A vote to destroy all big
bleeders? Any vote that can destroy IC members is a little crazy. I
object to this card on simple realism principle. If IC members were
immune, it would be an OK card.

The only card really done well was Elder Intervention. This card gives
everyone some decent anti-bleed intercept, and at an appropriate cost. I
almost wonder if this card was done by the same people that did the
others, it is so much better.

> Yes, bleeding can be dealt
> with by conventional means, but the Nosferatu, Brujah, Gangrel, Ravanos,
> Setities, and Assamites can neither bounce or effectively intercept an
> effective S&B deck

Nosferatu, Brujah, Gangrel, and Assamites all have rush defense. Ravnos
can have Rush (trap/drawing out beast/apparation) or combined
Chimerstry/Animalism intercept (which I have found to be _the_ best
intercept ever). Setites can do stealthed presence bleeds for blood
return or go (as I would suggest) to stealthed votes with blood gain
included. With serpentis, they can steal away the low or weak vamps.

(animalism intercept is not quite as good at stopping
> massed stealth as Auspex is), and while all these clans can fight, putting
> all your effort into fighting a S&B preadator means you are not hurting
> your prey, and you are just making it easier for your grand-preadator to
> gain 6 pool and then come for you next. At least with the threat of AI,
> the S&B deck needs to not kill quite as quickly.

The attack on your predator for survival is a large part of the game.
When you are put on the defense (whether passively, or aggressively),
your prey is always off. This will happen when any deck (rush, vote,
bleed, whatever) is doing well. But you need not finish of your predator
for your grandpredator. The best bet is too hold off and use
intimidation on your predator. They can't attack you if their predator

I completely agree with you about Justicar Retribution. The only vampires
that Justicar Retribution will burn are Inner Circle members and vamps
with Pulse of the Canille. Being that the card basically only burns IC
members, and IC members are supposed to be the most powerful of vampires,
that card is just plain brown wrong. Yes, IC members have 4 votes, but if
they are not in a vote deck, 4 votes won't save them from a Justicar
Retribution.

I also agree that Protected Recources is a overly powerful card for its
cost, but only in non bleed decks, and those generally are slower at
killing their prey than bleed decks are. Combat decks only reduce their
preys pool in a roundabout way, and vote decks are fairly easily shut down
by intercept or other vote decks. Without bleeding your prey, your path
to victory can be a very slow one, and PR can help to even the pace.

Archon Investigation, on the other hand, I find completely acceptable.
Yes, AI has the ability to burn your preadators vampire for very low cost,
but only if your preadator lets you. You never have to bleed someone for
more then 3, and there is generally no need to. If a good bleed deck
bleeds their prey for 3 an action, they will still kill them fairly
quickly. If they cannot manage to bleed their prey due to intercept or
bleed bounce, it does not mater how much you plan on bleeding, as it will
not hurt your prey, and AI has no effect. If you can manage to bleed your
prey, then 3 per bleed will kill them just fine. Bleeding someone for 6
or 7 points in one action is a fairly easy thing to arrange
(Govern+Conditioning), and I have always found it absurd to have to worry
about losing upwards of 25% (if not more) of your pool to one vampires
action. How bleeding someone for 7 in one action is in any way balanced
with beating up someones vampire or even voting someone 3 or 4 pool damage
has always completely escaped me. The fact that it is so easy to do so
much damage to someone always was cause for much concern, and AI solved
that problem. Yes, it could burn up your vampire, but you are never
forced to bleed for more than 3, ever. Again, if you are managing to
bleed your prey consistiently, then 3 is perfectly sufficient to kill
them. If you can't bleed your prey for whatever reason, then AI makes no
difference anyway. AI does not prevent you from trying to bleed your prey
for 7 or even 14 for that matter (IC member+Return to Innocence), but if
you are going to attempt that, there is a risk that you may fail and lose
a vampire in the process. It is a gamble that sometimes you may wish to
take (i.e. you have 1 vamp to act and your prey has 5 pool), but sometimes
when you gamble, you lose. If you don't want to risk your vampires
getting burned, then don't bleed for more than 3. The power of AI is not
that it can burn your preadators vampire, but that the threat of AI slows
down bleed decks to acceptable levels, comperable to other decks. Vote
decks generally will also only do 3 pool per action (KRC), and combat
decks are obtuse and fairly slow in their way to victory (ousting their
prey), so bleed decks working at 3 per bleed is just fine.

On 18 Jun 1996, Thomas R Wylie wrote:

> The Corrupter <sull...@cslab.uwlax.edu> wrote:

> >I think we are conflicting on definitions. By escalation, I mean that
> >the general power level of each strategy increases. I.e., a Brujah Rush
> >deck suddenly does a little more damage on all levels. In my opinion,
> >removal of wallpaper cards with useful cards would not necessarily escalate
> >strategy. If Brujah rush has new ways to do things, breadth can be
> >gained. For example, if Nossies never had Spawning Pool until now, its
> >inclusion would not be an escalation of power. Spawning Pool is costly,
> >a unique, and only useful in certain circumstances.

> Escalation can mean either increasing the average card power, or increasing
> the maximum card power. Stopping escalation of the latter sort is
> relatively easy, and generally desirable, but the occasional card will
> still slip through the cracks. Stopping escalation of the average card
> power is impossible without deliberately making bad cards that nobody
> plays with, which is sort of missing out on the point of expansions.

One can not increase the average card power without making bad cards.
This can be done as was done with Mercy for the Weak. This cards cost
decreases its effective power. It has its place in a number of decks, is
a good card, but is a weak (in terms of power) card. Disciplineless
cards are typically where the higher powered cards can have leave the
average power level of a set at relatively the same level. These cards
are weak, not bad, just as Fake Out is weak, not bad.

> And judging power isn't always easy. For example, as you point out,
> Setite stealth/bleed decks are different than existing ones. If it turns
> out that gaining pool for bleeds more than compensates for the loss in
> sheer bleeding power, then the new clan has just escalated the
> stealth/bleed strategy.

Not really. Presence based bleeding is far different than Dominate based
bleeding. You have introduced a new type of strategy. As Tremer can
be Dominate based Bruise-n-Bleed, Brujah can be Presence based. Neither
part can be looked at to talk about the whole.

I don't expect Presence S&B to be more powerful. It has less ways to get
the bleed thru (no Seduction, no Bonding), bleeds for less, and when it
does bleed for more, costs more blood (Followers of Set essentially pay 1
blood fro the equiavalent to Threats). The benefit? At superior
presence, pool gain.

If less bleed/more pool gain is more effective, it can't be called an
escalation, because it is essentially a different strategy from a new
clan. Were this strategy suddenly easily available to dominate (thru
pool gaining dominate bleed cards) that would be an escalation.

>If that's how you feel the game should be played, then >your preferences
>differ from mine. It irks me that given the way that AI >works, an IC
>member will virtually never use a bleed modifier of any >type. You don't
>find this odd? It seems ridiculous to me.

Yes, you are correct in stating that IC members will rarely use bleed
modifiers. Perhaps their power comes from the fact that they don't need
to use bleed modifiers, and can bleed for 3 each action on their own.

My main point about AI is that it slows down bleed decks to an acceptable
level, about equal to all other strategies. There is never any real need
to bleed someone for more than 3, ever. No one should ever have to take a
7 point bleed from one vampire, as it is too destructive to their ability
to play the game. Big bleeding is too quick as a way to victory, as not
only does further the basic victory contitions of the game (reducing your
preys pool to zero), but it also reduces your preys ability to resist as
well. Combat decks pretty much only reduce your targets ability to
resist. Direct damage vote decks work the same was as bleed decks, but not
as quickly, as a KRC deck will only cause 3 points of pool loss an action,
where a bleed deck (before the advent of AI) would cause 5-7 points of
pool loss per action. There are defenses against all decks, but in
situations where your defenses fail, before AI, bleed decks were far and
away more effective and damaging than any other type of deck per action.

Yes, you can stop vote decks with intercept or other votes, and you can
stop bleed decks with intercept and bleed bounce, and you can stop combat
with combat defense, but there will always be a situation where your
defenses fail. Against a combat deck, if your defenses fail, you get a
vampire torporized or (rarely) burned, which is usually no big deal in the
grand scheem of the game. Against a vote deck, if your defenses fail, you
lose 3 or 4 pool, which is pretty hefty, but not as bad as a bleed deck.
Before AI, when your defenses failed against a bleed deck, you would lose
6-8 pool, which is very bad, much worse than either of the other two
outcomes. This needed to be changed, and AI caused that change.

With AI in existance, bleed decks are brought down to the same level of
effectivness as other designs. Yes, you can no longer sneak bleed someone
for 7 without worry, but you should never have been able to do that anyway
(IMHO). I our local group, AI has been actually played only once (on
Queen Anne, none the less), but now people rarely bleed for more than 3 at
a time. The Bleed decks are still just as effective as they used to be,
but when they oust someone, it is not because they were faster at killing
than their prey was at defending. It is because they were crafty and
clever and had a well designed deck that killed people 3 pool at a time
(and ocasionaly more when they felt gutsy.)

eliminates it entirely. Any superior Conditioning can result in an
unpreventable burn of your vampire? Who on earth is going to base a
strategy around a big bleed anymore, or even risk a Conditioning?

AI's big problem is that it's an OOT, which is unstoppable without help

phase) then at least there would be some way to possibly deal with AI (on
top of the other things big bleeders have to worry about, such as Deflection,
intercept, rush combat, etc.). If AI were an OOT that cost nothing and
reduced a bleed to 3, I don't think there would be such a strong negative
reaction to it. Is it really your feeling that the burning the bleeder

if you're not holding AI, bleeder wins; if you are, bleeder loses.

Archon Investigation is just way too harsh for a card that cannot be
countered. Big bleeds, if they are a problem, could have (and should

Messages.Author: J. Hamblin
Messages.Body:
All right, all right. There's gotta be somebody out there who agrees
with Peter, right? Well, I do.

I think Archon Investigation (AI) is a great card. Why _should_ anyone
ever have to be bled for 10, anyway? I mean, granted, there are a lot of
anti-bleed strategies out there, but how can any clan that was not
designed for such defend against a well designed bleed deck (this is a
rhetorical question; I've seen some answers, and they're pretty feeb)?

AI gives everyone a good anti-bleed card and actually (*gasp*) makes
bleed decks have to worry about bleeding for insane amounts. Getting
bled for 3 at least once a turn is certainly sufficiently good to kill
your prey. Who wants to be ousted because their esoteric bleed defense
strategy takes a few turns to get going?

Stealth and Bleed (S&B) has always, in my mind, been Cheese Factor #1 in
this game. It's just so mindless, yet so incredibly effective. Ventrue
bleed isn't as effective. Vote-damage isn't as effective. And everyone
knows combat isn't as effective. So why doesn't everyone just make a
cheeze-supreme Malkavian S&B deck and make this game far less interesting
than it is? Because around here we've shamed everyone out of playing
stupid, boring decks. AI goes a long way towards evening out the playing
field for people less willing to risk alienating their peers.

losing 3. I don't see anything wrong with the pre-AI times at all.

> With AI in existance, bleed decks are brought down to the same level of
> effectivness as other designs.

AI didn't bring anything down but game balance. The cost is _totally_

devastating blow to your predator.

> (and ocasionaly more when they felt gutsy.)

deck? Most of your statements make me think so, but I'm not certain.

In any case, I don't agree with your assessment, but I doubt we'll change
each others mind. IMO, A card like AI is no problem, but AI itself needs
to pack more bite to the user. If the bleed were successful, AI would
still be a card that would cause people to think before bleeding, but it
would not be out of line like it is now. Jyhad is a card game in which
(excepting those few who slip thru) the cards all have appropriate cost;

second minion, or anything other than Potence, which you may very well
have if you are going to beat up somebody.

blocking a S+B deck keeps you alive. The first time you are bled (without
blocking), you get bled for 5 or 6 (moving 2 cards), that same turn the
next minion bleeds you for 3 or 4 (moving one card), and then you get bled
for 1 each by whatever is left over. You have just lost about10 pool, and
have effectively lost about 2 potential vampires, and thus the ability to
resist even further. If the bleed deck predator then discards a card at
the end of his turn, and plays a master card at the beginning of his turn,
you again get bled for 5 or 6 on the next turn (more if they happen to
have any defensive cards that they got to play). You have now lost
upwards of 15 pool, in 2 turns, in 3 or 4 actions. At this point, unless
you are a very speedy pool gain deck, or luckily managed to play a Minion
Tap that was not Sudden Reversaled, you are dead. If you are a Rush
Combat deck, you have managed to kill one of their vampires (at the cost
of possibly moving some of their cards), as you only have 1 or 2 vampires
having already lost 10 pool. Then you still die.

In any game where I stoicly decided not to block a S+B deck, I have died.
In any situation where anyone at the table I have been playing has stoicly
decided to try to hand jam the S+B deck by not blocking, they have died.
I just don't buy it as a viable defense. Perhaps by the time you are
dead, the S+B deck will have horrible hand jam for the next guy, but how
does that help you? You are dead.

I'm going to tackle your statements LIFO. If you are not playing
intercept, why even bother to block? All you do is help them cycle their
hand.

On to the point at hand.

The early pool loss (say from Govern the Unaligned, Conditioning) will be
large, but most bleed decks will start bleeding right away with a smaller
minion. If they are not, they are giving you time. This time will be
used to set up defense.

Let's look at the typical bleed deck (Malk, in this case). I will use
these assumption about the deck:

1/3 Stealth
1/3 Bleed
1/3 Master and Other (playable immediately)

An general hand will have, on (worst case) average 2 Stealth, 3 Bleed, 2
Other. With master cards, the first unblocked bleed will drain out the
bleed cards and an Other card (4 cards).

This is likely an early strike, and so won't as often hit very hard.
Even if it does, a loss of 6 pool early is better than 4 pool or more
every turn from multiple vampires.

At this point, the bleeder will be relegated to turn after turn of 1 or 0
bleed cards in hand. If 1/3 the deck is bleed, only 1 bleed card, versus
6 non-bleed cards will return. After playing that bleed card, it is
likely to have 7 non-bleed cards in hand. Not only is 1/3 of their deck
effectively dead weight, but they aren't likely to start discarding their
stealth (for fear they might need it) until they are clogging.

During this time, you had better not have been idle. Since you are not
playing an intercept deck (or else you would have been intercepting), you
should be getting to your bleed bounce, your rush, your whatever you do
to defend against bleeders. As another option, you could ignore your
predator and race to finish your prey. The important thing is, since you
are not blocking, unless you think someone else might (D) you, don't save
any blockers.

The 'not blocking' defense is a stall. It doesn't work by itself, but
gives you time to bring out your defense against bleed by giving you more
minion actions and clogging the stealth in your predator's hand. If you
don't have the bleed defense to bring out, you should rethink your deck.

You are pretty close, but my main problem with bleed is not that it is too
hard to defend against, but that if you fail (for whatever reason) to
defend against S+B, the consequences are FAR greater than if your defenses
fail against a combat deck, and somewhat greater than if your defenses
fail against a vote deck.

For example, in a 4 player game I played recently, I was playing a fairly
good rush combat deck, and my preadator was playing a weenie Presence
bleed deck (all little vamps with Presence that bleed for 2 or 3 each
action. If you kill 2 minions a turn with combat, he makes 3 new ones).
In the middle of the game, I had 14 pool and four good fighting vamps out,
and he had 4 stealthless 2 or 3 point weenie vamps (after I had killed 2
or 3) I felt I was in a good position and things were looking good for
me. He then played Misdirection (The "Channel" of Jyhad. I hate this
card. It should not exist. Sorry about the tangent.) to tap my two
untapped vamps, and with four 2 or 3 point vamps with only Presence, he
bled me for 14 points, using Social Charms and Aire of Elations. I was
imediately ousted. My deck had plenty of Deflections, WWEF, Rats Warning,
as well as AI, but by sheer dumb luck, none were in my hand and no one
Sudden Reversaled the Misdirection (Another card I hate. This card should
only exist because of Misdirection.), so I died. If I had a single one of
these cards in my hand, I would have lived, but it was just not in the
cards (Ooh. Sorry about that :-)

My point is not that I was unable to defend vs the bleed deck (I was
perfectly able to in a grand sense), but due to a series of obscure
events, my defenses failed, and was ousted when I had 14 pool and 4 good
vampires. If my Predator had been a combat deck, and I suffered the same
sort of critical defense failure, I would have had a couple vamps killed,
but as I a good deal of pool left, I could have kept fighting (i.e.
playing, even if from a hamstrung positon). If my preadator had been a
vote deck, I could have taken 12 pool loss at most (4 players, and my prey
had even more pool than me), but at least my Primogens and other players
could have helped swung things one way or another, but at worst I would
have lost 12 pool. As my prey was a bleed deck, I was killed in a swift
and merciless fashon.

My biggest problem with the S+B, or just plain Bleed strategy is that it
can be too swift and too decisive, and end the game way too quick, where
combat decks and non "All KRC" vote decks tend to drag the game out, and
let it develop. If your predator is a good bleed deck, and your defenses
fail, you are ousted VERY quickly. This is simply not the way I like to
play the game. To make a unneeded comparison to Magic (yeah, yeah, I
know...), Red direct damage decks are perfectly workable, can be easily
delt with, and are not particularly unbalancing, but I just don't like to
play with one or against one. I just think they are boring, and when they
work, the game ends real quick. I feel the same way about S+B decks (and
to a lesser extent non Stealthy Bleed decks). Generally, either they are
completely innefective ("Hey! I just happen to have 15 Deflections in my
deck. Cool."), or they oust their prey really quickly.

To tie this all together, yes, I think that Archon Investigation is
justifiable, as while it could easily be viewed as overkill (and is by
many), I just see it as a card that encourages the kind of play I prefer.
If this is not to a play groups liking, it is just a game, and it is very
easy to remove the card from a play enviornment with the agreement of the
players.

I completely agree here. The rare cards that get introduced need to not
be more powerful in terms of power per cost. If a card is powerful (like
Smiling Jack is), it is often held back in terms of cost, utility, and
general difficulties in bringing/keeping it out. Magic is plagued by
rare cards that are ultra destructive or useful for little cost, simply
because they are rare. This breeds the Mr. Suitcase effect. I like the
fact that I could sweep a table of people in my regular play circle with
my league deck (made from a _very_ limited random card selection). Few
games can do this, and I hope this doesn't change.

Most powerful cards are common and uncommon (Bum's Rush, Majesty) and this
allows new players to compete. One of the reasons I am glad that S&B
exists in Jyhad is that it gives new players a chance to be competitive
without needing to have rares and without needing to figure out extreme
combos early.

Here's to keeping rares on a power level roughly equal to the other
commonalities...

Perhaps if I put thing in a practical context I can convince some
people that AI is unneccessary as there is sufficient balance between S&B
and other concepts. I have four decks I play that are at various stages
of development and each has its own way of dealing with S&B and I would
like to summarize them for you. Perhaps seeing the application of a good
bleed defense will make it more clear.

My first deck is a Gangrel/Ravnos untap/intercept deck. This is
prolly my most efficient in defending from S&B due to its concentration
on intercept. First of all the deck is quick to set up. Usually by the
end of the opening game I can have two or three vampires with permanent
intercept (raven spys and sport bikes as well as KRCG) as well as being
virtually indestrucable (via lots of fortitude). On occasion I can get +3
intercept on a Ravnos forcing Malks to pour out those +stealths and then
Veiled Sight puts them right out of business. Ignis Fatuus does double
duty in taking some of that stealth off the offender and taking some of
the bite out of a bleed I can't (or won't) stop. The only problem i have
with the deck is that its a slow killer and can't rack up victory points
fast enough to win a game. Most of the damage is done through Army of
rats and peck bleeds with Earth control or Backways.

The second deck in my box is a Nos/Brujah/Assamite Rush deck I call
The Black Hand (however unrealistic without Sabbat). It's a
stealth/Rush/diablerie/vote combo that is still developing. It either
works fabulously or fails miserably but there is no doubt that it can
handle an S&B deck. Bum's Rush, Haven uncovered, Blood hunt, Archon to
get to you. Hidden Lurker, Psyche to stay on you. Quietus, potence,
celerity, Amaranth, Rit. of the bitter rose, and ALOT of weapons to make
you into breakfast. This deck is far from competitive though and has some
bugs that I have to work out. (mainly: its HUGE!)

The third deck is, guess what, an S&B deck! It is a Malk/Tremere S&B
with a touch of intercept/combat. It doesn't deliver those legendary
(bordering on fictional) +8 bleed +6 stealth kill bleeds with any
reliable frequency. What damage it does, it does with GREAT planning and
effort as well as a coup de grace for a bunch of turns as I assemble the cards
and await a moment of vulnerability in my prey. I like this tactic alot
as it demonstrates the patience and planning of truly great Methuselahs.
Unfotunately, AI has made this an unacceptable risk (potentially fatal).
As far as bleed defense there is a fair amount of bounce and intercept
including corpse minions and auspex. The combat portion of this deck is
designed more to make the vampires self sufficient (i.e. lots of steal
blood and hunting grounds) than to destroy or cripple vamps. It works on
a slow to build/hard to hit bleed with Malks and a survival based defense
with the Tremere. A very "vampire" deck.

My final deck is my oldest and favorite though it has gone through
recent tranformations. It is a Brujah/ventrue vote/diablerie deck. This
deck has ravaged many a S&B in its many incarnations. It has all the rush
combat stuff including archon (with camarilla exemp. ouch on those
obedience blockers). Again this deck tries to have a card efficient
combat base by concentrating on weapons and celerity (particularly Stakes
and Ivory bow). Potence plays a supporting role for enhanced damage but is
largely absent. As a secondary bleed defense and as secondary offense as
well there are a number of political actions including Banishments, Sabbat
threats, Archons, Parity Shift, Con. Boon, Cam. Exemplary, Kine Res.
Contested, and Bribes, voter captivation for quick pool gain. Master
cards include: Absolution of the Diabloist, Vulnerability, Pentex
Subversion, etc. Also there are two each of second trad. and Elder
intervention as well as 3 sport bikes and KRCG. If all this fails thre
are 3 Deflections in the deck as well. though bulky at 127 cards it fares
well.

These are the ways I handle bleed defense without AI. If you feel
this is insufficient I will tell you that at least two of these decks
have stood the test of time from the early days of Jyhad without any
particular fear of S&B. In fact the deck I most lose to is Gangrel Burn
decks. If this still doesn't convince you I suggest settling it in the
only way no one can argue about- in practice. You all can make your biggest
baddest S&B and I will play you. In fact I will even email everyone a
detailed list of my deck and crypt so everyone can plan accordingly and put
15 obidiences in their decks. If anyone wants to back me up, feel free.
We can sit everyone: pro-AI/anti-AI and settle it once and for all.

Doubly agreed. House rules anyone?

1) Doesn't burn the bleeder. Sends the bleeder to Torpor.

2) Doesn't burn the bleeder. Taps the bleeder and is placed on the bleeder.
While the card is on the minion, the minion cannot act. Any vampire may
take an action to pay 3 blood to burn the card.

is on the minion, the minion cannot bleed. Any vampire may burn the
card by calling a vote as a political action, which would be at +1 stealth.

4) Doesn't cost anything and doesn't burn the bleeder. Bleed is unsuccessful.

5) Cost 1. Bleed is unsuccessful, and you must pay X pool, where X is the
amount of the bleed had it been successful. If you cannot, you are
ousted, otherwise the bleeding minion is burned.

Comments and/or further ideas?

Besides the need for intercept that others have pointed out, you beat
Obedience by tapping or negating the defender: Misdirection, Incriminating
Videotape, Pentex Subversion, Horrific Countenance. Most Rush decks won't
carry these because they "want to be blocked", but just wanted to point
out that there are things to counter Obedience. There is a good chance
that a Rush deck will have a vampire old enough that it cannot be Obedienced.
Basilia and Thetmes are the likely candidates.

Of more relevance, the chances that an effective S&B deck will be holding
enough Obedience to stop a Haven Uncovered attack (which will typically
generate at least 3 attempted combats) is quite low. If the S&Ber is
typically holding 3 Obedience, then there's only 4 hand slots left for
Stealth/Bleed (presuming you don't mind missing your Master phase). That's
either 3 Stealth cards (+4 stealth) and Conditioning (4-5 bleed), or 2
stealth (+3 stealth) and GtU+Conditioning (6-7 bleed). Any decent intercept
deck should be able to stop a +3 stealth bleed (given that Elder Intervention
is already +2 intercept) and should have a good shot at a +4 stealth bleed.
The +4 stealth bleed is for 4-5, which is only 1-2 more than AI costs, and
I think all the pro-AI people were screaming about 7-10 point bleeds, not
4-5 point bleeds.

The point is that if you hold enough Obedience to stop Rush, you won't be
able to S&B very well.

>there needed to be some kind of anti-bleed card as around

My problem with AI is this:

Yes, 1 or 2 giant bleeds can often oust in a way that's very unsatifying,
and frustrating for the oustee.

BUT, a successful AI hoses the bleeder as surely as the big bleed.

So when a bleeder does a big bleed against someone using AI for defense,
somebody will go home frustrated. It's a no-win situation.

The more fundamental problem is that WotC is trying to fix a general
problem (big whonker bleeds) with a specific card. But with over 500
cards, this only works if the card is so good that it appears in virtually
every game. But if it's that good, it's probably a spoiler too, and
you've just replaced one problem with another. For an example, look at
Necropotence from magic - an attempt to control those boring blue/white
decks just created another new type you see endlessly.

A better kind of fix for big bleeds would be a rules change - like not
allowing you to combine +bleed action modifiers with + bleed actions. I
assume WotC avoids this because of the confusion multiple rules would
engender.

Fundamental aspects of CCGs should be fixed with rules changes, or lived
with.
